title: From the FBI to Meta’s Muse: What Data Exposure and AI Permissions Mean for Holiday Shopping Privacy.
summary: The NCIC investigation and a separate FBIJobs.gov data claim are not linked to AI or shopping scams. Still, they underscore why personal data, app permissions, and urgent messages deserve scrutiny.
body_markdown:
The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its[National Crime Information Center (NCIC)](https://apnews.com/article/fbi-database-ncic-hack-d066cff87a64a564db0a00172c124972) , a nationwide law-enforcement database that includes records on fugitives, missing people, criminal histories, and stolen property. Early reporting said the scope and impact were unclear. This follows a separate September incident: ShinyHunters claimed FBIJobs.gov was compromised, and the FBI said it was investigating. A sample of the alleged data reviewed by Reuters reportedly included employee names, addresses, phone numbers, birth dates, Social Security numbers, and emergency contacts ([USA Today/Reuters](https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/crime/2026/09/23/fbi-data-hack-shinyhunters/91908431007/) ). The two incidents have not been linked.


Neither FBI incident has been connected to AI or consumer shopping scams. Separately, the[FBI warns](https://www.fbi.gov/contact-us/field-offices/sanfrancisco/news/fbi-warns-of-increasing-threat-of-cyber-criminals-utilizing-artificial-intelligence) that criminals use AI to make targeted phishing and social-engineering attacks faster and more convincing, and to create voice or video impersonations. That distinction matters: a data breach and an AI-assisted scam are different risks, even though exposed personal details can make an unexpected message seem more credible.


Separately, reports about Meta’s Muse raise questions about what an AI agent can access through app permissions. Some employee testers reportedly saw Muse refer to private app activity or apparent financial details.


[The Guardian reported](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/sep/28/metas-ai-agent-muse-home-address) that Muse sent a Marketplace buyer the home address he had provided for pickup after he selected “Allow Always,” believing the agent would still ask before accepting offers.[Surfshark’s analysis](https://surfshark.com/research/chart/meta-muse-ai-chatbots) found Muse’s App Store disclosures may cover 31 of Apple’s 35 data categories; that does not prove Muse collects every type. Meta separately disputed a claim that Muse accessed Apple Messages with Full Disk Access turned off, saying the integration requires that permission and an enabled connector, according to[TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2026/09/30/meta-disputes-claim-that-muse-read-a-users-private-messages-without-permission/) .


Although these incidents have not been formally linked, together they point to the broader[“Digital Grid”](https://www.gendigital.com/blog/insights/leadership-perspectives/major-outages-scams) : connected apps, devices, platforms, and services where sensitive information and permissions can cross boundaries. Because this grid has its own vulnerabilities, it’s important to review what you've allowed agents to access or do, and verify any urgent requests you receive, even if they seem to arrive from a legitimate channel.


## Black Friday scams exploit urgency and confusion


The shopping rush gives criminals an opening. Scammers often adapt messages to current events and consumer concerns. An alert claiming an AI shopping assistant must be reconnected, or that a retailer has changed its security settings, could send shoppers to a fake login page or ask for personal information. That’s a foreseeable scenario, not evidence of a documented Muse-related scam trend. The[FTC warns holiday shoppers](https://consumer.ftc.gov/consumer-alerts/2026/11/how-avoid-holiday-shopping-scams-your-search-results) about fake stores, impersonation, and other online shopping scams.


Be skeptical of unexpected messages claiming that:


- Your account needs to be reconnected to an AI shopping assistant.
- A payment failed and your card details must be entered again.
- A limited-time deal will disappear unless you buy immediately.
- A package is delayed until you pay an extra fee or confirm personal information.
- Your bank or retailer needs a password or verification code to secure your account.


Don’t use links or phone numbers in unexpected messages. Open the retailer’s official app or type its website address yourself. The[FTC recommends going directly to a company’s known website](https://consumer.ftc.gov/consumer-alerts/2026/11/how-avoid-holiday-shopping-scams-your-search-results) and[researching unfamiliar sellers](https://consumer.ftc.gov/consumer-alerts/2025/11/how-avoid-online-shopping-scam-holiday-season) .


Never send a password or one-time security code in response to an unexpected text, email, or phone call. Enter a legitimate code only in the company’s official app or website when you initiated the login or transaction. When you use an AI tool to shop, check which accounts it can access and what actions it can take. Review purchases, payment methods, and connected accounts yourself before authorizing an agent to act.


## How to protect your information this holiday season


- **Review app permissions.** Check which apps can access notifications, your screen, microphone, files, contacts, and location. Turn off access you don’t need.
- **Check connected accounts.** Review integrations for AI assistants, shopping apps, and browser extensions. Remove connections you no longer use.
- **Protect important logins.** Use unique passwords and turn on multifactor authentication or passkeys where available.
- **Keep devices and apps updated.** Install updates through official settings or app stores.
- **Monitor your financial accounts.** Turn on transaction alerts and review statements for unfamiliar activity.
- **Slow down.** Verify unexpected requests independently before you click, pay, or share information.


## How Gen can help


Good privacy habits start with knowing what you’re sharing and limiting access to what’s necessary. If you’re concerned about personal information exposed on data broker sites,[Norton Privacy Monitor Assistant](https://us.norton.com/products/privacy-monitor-assistant) scans supported sites and can submit removal requests.


No product can replace careful permission choices or guarantee that an AI service will handle information exactly as you expect. But you can make more informed choices: check access before you grant it, keep sensitive information out of prompts, and verify unexpected requests through a trusted channel.


AI should make everyday tasks easier—not leave you wondering what it knows. A few minutes spent reviewing permissions and shopping habits can help you stay in control of your information this holiday season.
